summary: This informational memo discusses requirements for renumbering with stateless DHCPv6. Hosts using stateless address autoconfiguration get their address automatically but need DHCPv6 for settings such as DNS and NTP, so the document describes how those settings should be updated when a network changes.

eli5.summary: If a neighbourhood changes its street numbers, everyone must learn the new ones. This document discusses how computers should refresh extra network settings when that happens.

questions: how do ipv6 hosts update dns settings after renumbering
how do ipv6 hosts get dns settings
what happens to configuration when a network renumbers
why cant stateless dhcpv6 tell hosts about changes
subtitle: How IPv6 hosts learn about network changes when using stateless configuration

tldr.problem: IPv6 hosts can configure their own addresses automatically, but they also need DNS, NTP, and other settings from DHCPv6. When a network renumbers or settings change, these hosts have no way to find out.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC identifies two scenarios (site renumbering and configuration changes) and lists requirements for a solution, plus candidate approaches such as adding timeout lifetimes, using router announcements as hints, or adding a multicast reconfiguration mechanism.
tldr.outcome: This is a problem statement requesting solutions; the RFC does not specify a fix but lays out the problem and constraints for protocol designers to address in follow-on work.

today: RFC 4076 is an informational problem statement. It does not define a solution but lays out the requirements and candidate approaches. Follow-on RFCs in the DHC and DKIM working groups have addressed aspects of this problem, though a complete solution that preserves full statelessness remains a challenge in IPv6 deployment.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
IPv6 introduced Stateless Address Autoconfiguration, which lets hosts automatically configure their own IP address and default router by listening to router advertisements. This is lighter-weight than DHCP because the host does not need a server to assign an address and the server does not need to maintain state about each client.

However, autoconfiguration does not provide DNS servers, NTP servers, or other configuration settings. To get those, hosts can use the stateless variant of DHCPv6, which works similarly: the server sends configuration parameters (like DNS server addresses) when the client requests them, but the server does not track which addresses it has handed out or maintain a lease database.

The problem: when the network changes those configuration settings—either because the site is renumbering (getting a new IP prefix from its ISP) or because a DNS server moved to a new address—there is no mechanism to tell stateless DHCPv6 clients. The hosts continue using stale information.
sections.eli5: When your home network gets a new address range, or moves to a new ISP, it needs to tell computers about the new DNS server. But stateless DHCP doesn't have a way to push that information, so computers keep using the old addresses.

sections.title: Renumbering Scenarios
sections.content:
Site renumbering: IPv6 currently has no provider-independent address space; all sites receive addresses from their ISP using provider-assigned space. If a site changes ISPs, it must renumber. Hosts using stateless autoconfiguration will learn the new address prefix from router advertisements, but they will not learn updated DNS, NTP, or other settings from stateless DHCPv6.

Settings changes: An administrator may need to change configuration settings without renumbering—for example, adding a new DNS server, removing an old one, or changing the DNS search path. Hosts will not discover these changes.

In contrast, hosts using full (stateful) DHCPv6 typically discover updates when they renew their address lease, because the server can include new configuration in the renewal. Stateless DHCPv6 has no such renewal cycle.
sections.eli5: Two things can happen: the whole site gets a new IP prefix (renumbering), or just specific settings like DNS servers change. Either way, hosts with old configuration settings don't learn about it.

sections.title: Requirements for a Solution
sections.content:
The RFC identifies requirements any solution must meet:

  • Support planned renumbering: The solution should ideally handle both planned events (where the administrator knows in advance) and unplanned ones (like an ISP outage forcing a provider change).
  • Maintain security: No new security risks should be introduced to stateless DHCPv6.
  • Update non-address options: The mechanism must work for DNS, NTP, and other settings even if the network is not renumbering.
  • Preserve stateless operation: It is desirable that the DHCPv6 server still does not need to maintain per-client state.
sections.eli5: Any fix should work for both planned and surprise network changes, shouldn't break security, should work for any kind of setting change (not just IP), and ideally shouldn't force servers to remember who each client is.

sections.title: Candidate Solution Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC outlines four candidate approaches for protocol designers to pursue:

Multicast reconfiguration: Add a reconfigure mechanism like the one in full DHCPv6, but adapted to work with multicast messages so the server does not need to know client addresses. This could handle both planned and unplanned events but may require significant protocol changes.

Configuration lifetimes: Extend DHCPv6 to include a lifetime or validity period for each configuration option (DNS, NTP, etc.). Clients would re-request settings when the lifetime expires. With short lifetimes, this could handle unplanned events quickly, but at the cost of extra traffic; with long lifetimes, it primarily handles planned events that the administrator coordinates with network planning.

Router advertisement hints: Use router advertisements as a signal that the client should re-request configuration. For example, when a router detects a new prefix or address, it could set a flag in the RA asking clients to refresh their DHCPv6-learned settings. This does not directly detect DNS or NTP changes, but it helps with renumbering events.

O-flag semantics: Change how the "O" (Other configuration) flag in router advertisements works, so toggling it could signal that clients should request new information.
sections.eli5: Possible fixes: have routers broadcast a "refresh your settings" message (but that's hard without addresses), give DNS settings an expiration time (like DHCP addresses have), use router advertisement changes as hints to ask for new settings, or repurpose an existing flag in router advertisements.

sections.title: Security and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that security is important. Whatever mechanism is chosen must not open the door to attacks such as spoofed configuration messages or injection of false DNS servers. Existing DHCPv6 and router advertisement security mechanisms should be reused.

The RFC also notes that the scope of the problem could extend beyond stateless DHCPv6: even in full DHCPv6, only address options have explicit lifetimes; other options like DNS do not automatically expire or force a re-check. However, full DHCPv6 clients often renew their address lease, giving the server an opportunity to push new non-address settings. Stateless DHCPv6 clients have no such renewal.

Security considerations for renumbering events themselves (such as updating firewalls and ACLs to reflect server moves or removals) are noted as out of scope for this document but important for follow-up work.
sections.eli5: Fixing this shouldn't let attackers inject fake DNS servers. Also, the problem isn't just with stateless DHCP; even full DHCP doesn't have a way to expire settings. That's for future work to handle.
